title: How do you track CPD across multiple professional bodies?
description: How to track CPD, CPE and CLE for staff registered with different professional bodies: build a rules register, record evidence once, and map it to each body.
shortAnswer: CPD across multiple professional bodies is tracked by building a register of each body's rules (hours or units, period, mandatory categories, caps, carryover, evidence and retention), recording every learning activity once with its evidence, mapping that record to each body the person belongs to, and monitoring progress against each body's own period so gaps are found months before renewal or audit, not after.
keyTakeaways: Every body counts differently: hours or units, annual or triennial periods, different period start dates and different mandatory categories.
Record each activity once, with evidence, then map it to every body that may accept it. Do not keep separate logs per body.
Caps, carryover rules and verification requirements decide whether an activity counts, not just its length.
Retention periods differ by body and are often longer than the CPD period itself.
The individual practitioner usually holds the obligation. The organization's job is to make compliance easy and visible.

sections.heading: Why is tracking CPD across professional bodies difficult?

blocks.text: Tracking is difficult because each professional body sets its own unit of measure, period, mandatory topics, limits and evidence rules, and many organizations employ people registered with several bodies at once. The terms also differ: continuing professional development (CPD), continuing professional education (CPE) for accountants and tax practitioners in some markets, and continuing legal education (CLE) for lawyers in the United States. See [CPD vs CPE vs CLE](/compare/cpd-vs-cpe-vs-cle) and [continuing professional development](/glossary/continuing-professional-development).

The examples below, drawn from rules already documented in this library, show how far the variables differ even between bodies in the same country. They illustrate the design problem and are not a complete statement of any body's rules; check each body's current requirements.

sections.heading: How do CPD rules differ between professional bodies?

blocks.text: CPD rules differ on at least six variables: amount, unit, period, mandatory content, limits and evidence. The comparison shows examples from several markets.

Details for each are on the library's regulation pages, such as [NSW solicitor CPD](/regulations/nsw-solicitor-cpd-requirements) and [US CPA CPE requirements](/regulations/us-cpa-cpe-requirements).

Carryover is a good example of hidden variation. The California Board of Accountancy allows no carryover of CPE ([California Board of Accountancy](https://www.dca.ca.gov/cba/licensees/cequickref.shtml)), while the Law Society of NSW allows a limited carryover of units earned between January and March. A tracking system that assumes one rule will misstate compliance.

sections.heading: What are the steps to track CPD across bodies?

blocks.text: Set up tracking in six steps. The rules register comes before any system configuration.

items: **Identify who is registered where.** List every person with a registration, license or membership that carries a CPD obligation, the body, the registration number and the renewal date. Include people with more than one.

**Build a rules register.** For each body, record the fields in the template below from the body's own published rules, with the date you checked and a review date. Assign an owner to watch for rule changes.

**Record activities once.** Capture each learning activity with date, provider, duration, topic, format, learning outcome and evidence (certificate, attendance record, assessment result). Recording once avoids conflicting versions.
**Map each activity to bodies.** For each person, apply each relevant body's rules to decide whether, and how much, the activity counts: category, unit conversion, caps and verification standard.

**Monitor against each period.** Show each person and their manager progress against each body's period, with alerts well before period end. Periods often differ: a financial year, a calendar year, a triennium starting at registration.
**Prepare for audit.** Keep evidence for the longest retention period that applies, and test retrieval by sampling a few people each year as if a body had selected them for audit.

sections.heading: What should a CPD rules register contain?

blocks.text: A rules register should capture, for each body, everything needed to decide whether a given activity counts and whether a person is on track. Use these fields.

sections.heading: Who is responsible for CPD compliance: the individual or the employer?

blocks.text: For most professional registrations the individual practitioner holds the CPD obligation, but the employer often carries the consequences when a registration lapses. The Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (Ahpra), as an example, states that practitioners in any form of practice must participate regularly in CPD relevant to their scope of practice ([Ahpra](https://www.ahpra.gov.au/Registration/Registration-Standards/CPD.aspx)). Some financial services regimes, such as the Insurance Distribution Directive's annual training requirement, place obligations on firms as well. The practical answer is shared: individuals own their record; the organization provides the system, the alerts and the qualifying learning, and checks that people in registered roles remain registered. See [Ahpra CPD registration standards](/regulations/ahpra-cpd-registration-standards).

sections.heading: What are the most common CPD tracking errors?

items: Counting total hours while missing a mandatory category or annual minimum.
Ignoring caps on self-study or reading, so recorded hours exceed countable hours.
Using one period for everyone instead of each body's period.
Keeping attendance confirmations a body does not accept as evidence.
Deleting records after the period ends, before the retention period expires.
Not re-checking rules after a body changes them, for example when NASBA and AICPA revised the CPE standards effective August 1, 2026 ([NASBA](https://www.nasbaregistry.org/the-standards)).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry records learning against defined outcomes and the requirements they serve, so one activity can be mapped to several bodies' rules without duplicate records. Rule sources are versioned, so a change to a body's requirements shows which people and records are affected.

faqs.q: Can one learning activity count for more than one professional body?
faqs.a: Often yes, if it meets each body's rules on topic, format and evidence. A person registered as both an accountant and a tax agent may claim the same relevant activity with both, subject to each body's categories and caps. Record the activity once and map it to each body rather than logging it twice.

faqs.q: Should the employer keep CPD records or the individual?
faqs.a: Both, where possible. The individual usually holds the legal obligation and must produce records if audited. The employer benefits from holding a copy because it shows the organization supports compliance and can confirm people in registered roles remain eligible to practice.

faqs.q: How long should CPD records be kept?
faqs.a: As long as the longest applicable rule requires. Examples in this library range from three years for NSW solicitors to five years for nurses, midwives and Australian tax agents. Retention often runs past the end of the CPD period, so do not delete records when a period closes.

faqs.q: What is the difference between CPD hours and CPE credits?
faqs.a: They are units set by different bodies. Some count clock hours; others define a credit by minutes of participation. The AICPA and NASBA standards, for example, equate fifty minutes of participation in a formal learning program with one CPE credit. Convert using each body's own definition.
